newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-IBJ readies for big push under Big Bang.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-IBJ readies for big push under Big Bang.

text.p: The Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ) is hoping for greater business opportunities arising from the nation's "Big Bang" financial reforms.

"The reforms will support what we have intended to do. We see the Big Bang coming at a good time and giving us good business opportunities," Yoshiyuki Fujisawa, IBJ's deputy president, said in a recent interview with Reuters.
However, analysts warn of tough times ahead for the country's biggest long-term credit bank, which raises funds through bank debenture issues and provides long-term loans.
An analyst said: "IBJ's size is too small to make it a major global player. I cannot expect a rosy future for the bank if it remains as it is amid growing competition."
Japanese long-term credit banks, including IBJ, have been restricted from venturing into retail banking.

While they are allowed to issue virtually unlimited amounts of bank debentures as a means of raising funds and to provide long-term finance to key industries, deregulation over the past decade has eroded these advantages. Commercial banks are now allowed to extend long-term loans.
Another analyst expects IBJ to look to merge with a securities house.

"In particular, IBJ may want to merge with Nomura Securities Co Ltd... They would be a great couple if they were to merge," the analyst said, adding that IBJ is not interested in the retail banking business.
Fujisawa said that IBJ would not be interested in mergers which would hurt its efficiency, but would be interested in setting up a holding company.

Japanese banks are interested in financial holding firms because the corporate structure of such firms allows them to manage more flexibly through the setting of different pay scales and by cutting unprofitable operations, analysts say.
Holding companies control one or more other firms but do not themselves engage in a specific business.

"We may come across a situation where we had better have a retail network for our securities business. In that case, we will consider making business alliances with strong partners or we may want them to become affiliated with us," he said.

Last month, Japan unveiled a blueprint to implement "Big Bang" reforms aimed at breaking down barriers between segmented financial sectors to boost competition and lure back business which has left for less regulated pastures by 2000.

As a part of the reforms, the Finance Ministry is expected to submit a bill allowing for the setting up of financial holding firms in an extraordinary session of parliament this autumn. The Japanese government will also make a final decision on tax changes related to holding firms.
Fujisawa said that IBJ will pay close attention to discussions over tax changes in deciding whether to set up a holding company.

Analysts say that IBJ has already worked out a bold plan to become a global investment bank engaging in corporate finance and securities business for corporate and institutional customers in the wholesale market.
IBJ has set up units and affiliates needed to handle the underwriting and asset management business, such as securities, investment trust and trust banking arms and an investment advisory affiliate.

Fujisawa said that those subsidiaries are still relatively new but have already posted good results in their respective fields of business. The next obstacle is how they will build on their expertise to offer high quality services, he said.

Some analysts say, however, that it may be difficult for IBJ to take risks in expanding its investment banking business in the future as its profitability is low compared with its rivals both at home and abroad.
